### tech-news/google-antitrust-case-key-facts-and-testimony.md

Title: Google Antitrust Case: Key Facts and Testimony
Summary: Overview of Google's antitrust trial, including CEO testimony, financial data on default search engine deals, chat log destruction, and legal arguments regarding monopoly practices.

The U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google stems from a 2020 claim over its dominance in the online search market, separate from a January filing by the Department of Justice and eight states to halt its anticompetitive scheme. The government argues Google uses platforms and deals to block competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing necessary data. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified, defending tactics including deals to make Google the default search engine, stating that being the default is a desirable business practice, not illegal. 

Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine across platforms, including attempts to preinstall Chrome on iPhones. Approximately $18 billion of this total went directly to Apple, with the deal in place since 2003. Pichai claimed the decision to pay for default status was made with the consumer in mind to gather data and improve the search engine. A 2007 internal email revealed that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they performed 15% more searches, dropping 27% when they switched away.

Regarding preinstallation, Pichai admitted in 2018 to attempting to convince Tim Cook to preinstall Google services on every iOS device to create an inseparable connection between Google and Apple services, though Tim Cook refused. Google also faced accusations in February of systematically destroying internal chat messages despite a litigation hold, though Pichai later took action to change the chat history default to comply. 

Legal arguments highlighted hypocrisy, noting that while Google denounced Microsoft's 2005 default search engine monopoly, Google's own actions worsened the problem. The DOJ argued that changes to defaults worsen issues, as most users do not change defaults, and noted that competitors like DuckDuckGo, Brave, and Bing use similar arguments against Google's deals with Apple. The case is expected to continue for several weeks and is considered the biggest tech antitrust fight since the U.S. trial against Microsoft in the 1990s. If ruled against Google, the company may be required to change behavior and share APIs with third-party developers.

### tech-news/google-search-dominance-data-practices-and-manipulation.md

Title: Google Search dominance, data practices, and manipulation allegations
Summary: Examines Google's competitive advantages through data scale and ubiquity, its data collection practices, and controversies regarding search result manipulation versus official denials.

Google's dominance is attributed to scale, longevity, ubiquity, and unmatched user data collection, which includes search queries, smart speaker inputs, and clicked ads or results for personalization. Its central index exceeds 100 million gigabytes, updated by machine learning to rank results by quality and usability rather than just keyword presence. Data volume has grown from approximately 9 ZB in 2013 to 120 ZB in 2023, driven by live information. While some queries yield more ads due to keyword matching, Google denies pushing users toward monetizable subjects or allowing ad systems to affect organic results, citing separate meaning matching processes for organic queries. Kent Walker argues Google is preferred due to quality, not default status, noting user efforts to switch defaults on Firefox and Windows. Controversies include allegations by Megan Gray that Google manipulated 'children's clothing' queries to promote 'NIKOLAI-brand kidswear' for ad revenue, a claim Google denied. Additionally, Wired removed an article on this manipulation; Grey, a former DuckDuckGo VP, admitted she may have misinterpreted evidence but maintained Google manipulates search to maximize revenue. Bing has attempted to compete with generative AI chatbot explanations but faced pricing failures, such as ignoring user constraints for bike prices.

### tech-news/apple-defends-google-search-deal-in-court-there-wasn-t-a.md

Title: Apple defends Google Search deal in court: 'There wasn't a valid alternative'
Summary: Eddy Cue testified in US v. Google that Apple had no valid alternative to Google's search engine, negotiated the 2016 ISA with Sundar Pichai, and argues switching is easy despite ISA restrictions.

Eddy Cue testified in US v. Google, the antitrust trial over Google's search business, defending the Information Services Agreement (ISA) which makes Google the default search engine on Apple devices. The ISA has been in place since 2002, with Cue negotiating the current iteration with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. During renegotiation, Apple sought a higher revenue percentage from users directed to the search engine, while Pichai wanted to keep the deal as is; they compromised on an undisclosed number.

Cue stated there was no valid alternative to Google at the time and there still isn't one, arguing Apple never seriously considered switching providers or building its own search product. Apple also argues that switching search engines is easy, contradicting DuckDuckGo's claims, and downplays Google's financial role in the deal, citing platform appeal instead. Additionally, Apple claims better privacy than Google and notes that Google integration was a key Safari innovation since before 2003.

The defense maintained that Alameda was a successful hedge fund and FTX an innovative company, not a Ponzi scheme, and claimed legal business practices were followed. He argued he was not guilty, stating he built two billion-dollar businesses and did not steal money, offering to give up personal wealth to make customers whole.

Witness testimony began with Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London, who testified that he invested in FTX in 2021, trading Bitcoin and Dogecoin, and failed to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8. Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, testified that he joined Alameda and FTX after Bankman-Fried persuaded him to leave Jane Street; Yedidia claimed legal immunity because he feared his code contributed to a crime. Binance pulled out $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX.

### tech-news/google-search-dominance-data-practices-and-manipulation.md

Title: Google Search dominance, data practices, and manipulation allegations
Summary: Examines Google's competitive advantages through data scale and ubiquity, its data collection practices, and controversies regarding search result manipulation versus official denials.

Google's dominance is attributed to scale, longevity, ubiquity, and unmatched user data collection, which includes search queries, smart speaker inputs, and clicked ads or results for personalization. Its central index exceeds 100 million gigabytes, updated by machine learning to rank results by quality and usability rather than just keyword presence. Data volume has grown from approximately 9 ZB in 2013 to 120 ZB in 2023, driven by live information. While some queries yield more ads due to keyword matching, Google denies pushing users toward monetizable subjects or allowing ad systems to affect organic results, citing separate meaning matching processes for organic queries. Kent Walker argues Google is preferred due to quality, not default status, noting user efforts to switch defaults on Firefox and Windows. Controversies include allegations by Megan Gray that Google manipulated 'children's clothing' queries to promote 'NIKOLAI-brand kidswear' for ad revenue, a claim Google denied. Additionally, Wired removed an article on this manipulation; Grey, a former DuckDuckGo VP, admitted she may have misinterpreted evidence but maintained Google manipulates search to maximize revenue. Bing has attempted to compete with generative AI chatbot explanations but faced pricing failures, such as ignoring user constraints for bike prices.

### tech-news/helena-world-chronicle-files-antitrust-suit-against-google.md

Title: Helena World Chronicle files antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet
Summary: Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action lawsuit in U.S. District Court in D.C. accusing Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior under the Sherman Act, alleging they siphon off content, readers, and ad revenue through AI and older technologies.

Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas publisher owning two weekly newspapers, filed a class action lawsuit in U.S. District Court in D.C. against Google and Alphabet, alleging anticompetitive behavior under the Sherman Act. The suit claims Google siphons off publisher content, readers, and ad revenue through AI technologies and older methods like Featured Snippets and Search Generative Experience (SGE). The publisher argues that Google's Knowledge Graph, which launched in May 2012 and contained 500 billion facts by 2020, misappropriated data from publishers, causing them to lose billions of dollars. The case cites a 2023 News Media Alliance report and a Washington Post article stating Google's Bard AI was trained on news publications, which were the third-largest category of training data. The suit alleges changing AdSense rates and the improper spoliation of evidence via Google's destruction of chat messages, referencing the recent Epic Games antitrust win. It seeks damages and an injunction requiring Google to obtain publisher consent to use website data for training AI products, including rivals' AI, and allowing opt-out publishers to appear in search results. The U.S. lawsuit coincides with the Justice Department's suit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies. Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act for class-wide monetary and injunctive relief. Hausfeld law firm states Google's scheme causes profound harm to competition, consumers, labor, and a democratic free press. Google recently reached an agreement with the Canadian government to pay $73.5 million annually to news organizations, though negotiations with Meta remain unresolved.

### tech-news/google-antitrust-case-key-facts-and-testimony.md

Title: Google Antitrust Case: Key Facts and Testimony
Summary: Overview of Google's antitrust trial, including CEO testimony, financial data on default search engine deals, chat log destruction, and legal arguments regarding monopoly practices.

The U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google stems from a 2020 claim over its dominance in the online search market, separate from a January filing by the Department of Justice and eight states to halt its anticompetitive scheme. The government argues Google uses platforms and deals to block competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing necessary data. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified, defending tactics including deals to make Google the default search engine, stating that being the default is a desirable business practice, not illegal. 

Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine across platforms, including attempts to preinstall Chrome on iPhones. Approximately $18 billion of this total went directly to Apple, with the deal in place since 2003. Pichai claimed the decision to pay for default status was made with the consumer in mind to gather data and improve the search engine. A 2007 internal email revealed that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they performed 15% more searches, dropping 27% when they switched away.

Regarding preinstallation, Pichai admitted in 2018 to attempting to convince Tim Cook to preinstall Google services on every iOS device to create an inseparable connection between Google and Apple services, though Tim Cook refused. Google also faced accusations in February of systematically destroying internal chat messages despite a litigation hold, though Pichai later took action to change the chat history default to comply. 

Legal arguments highlighted hypocrisy, noting that while Google denounced Microsoft's 2005 default search engine monopoly, Google's own actions worsened the problem. The DOJ argued that changes to defaults worsen issues, as most users do not change defaults, and noted that competitors like DuckDuckGo, Brave, and Bing use similar arguments against Google's deals with Apple. The case is expected to continue for several weeks and is considered the biggest tech antitrust fight since the U.S. trial against Microsoft in the 1990s. If ruled against Google, the company may be required to change behavior and share APIs with third-party developers.
</notes>

Title: SBF's $5B offer to Trump and FTX's rise and fall
Summary: This note covers Sam Bankman-Fried's reported $5 billion offer to Donald Trump to cancel his presidential run, his background with Michael Lewis, FTX's marketing and trading growth, and the subsequent collapse and legal proceedings.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF), the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of FTX, reportedly offered Donald Trump $5 billion to cancel his presidential re-run; no wire transfer was confirmed. SBF pleaded not guilty to seven charges of fraud and conspiracy in the Manhattan Federal Court trial.

Michael Lewis's book 'Going Infinite' is set to debut on the first day of SBF's trial. In a 60 Minutes interview, Lewis defended SBF's business practices, claiming FTX would have remained profitable without customer deposit runs.

FTX raised approximately $2 billion, including $1 billion in 2021, from backers including Sequoia, Temasek, and Tiger Global. To lend legitimacy, FTX secured marketing deals with Tom Brady ($55 million) and Steph Curry ($35 million). Anna Wintour contacted SBF via Zoom to sponsor her Met Costume Ball. FTX trading volume climbed to $15 billion per day. SBF also met with Mitch McConnell to fund Republican candidates offsetting Trump's influence.

The company's cryptocurrency valuations fell sharply after being based on speculation rather than banked value. SBF has been denied bail and is widely blamed by crypto investors for losses at Alameda Research and FTX. CEO Ayelet Noff of Sliced Brand criticized SBF, stating he lacked management experience, delayed crypto adoption by 1-2 years, and damaged the community. Title: Sam Bankman-Fried trial: Opening statements and witness testimony
Summary: A summary of the opening statements and initial witness testimony in the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, covering the prosecution's allegations of fraud and the defense's arguments regarding startup risks and restitution.

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, jury selection concluded, and both sides presented opening statements before witnesses took the stand. Prosecutor Thane Rehn characterized Bankman-Fried as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims, contrasting his public image as a 'crypto boy' genius. Rehn alleged that Bankman-Fried oversaw a thriving FTX exchange, traveled internationally, and socialized with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David while assuring customers their funds were safe. The prosecution claimed Bankman-Fried built this image on lies, allegedly stealing customer funds to finance a jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Prosecutors argued Bankman-Fried used Alameda Research, a hedge fund he owned, and his girlfriend Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda) as a front to gain secret access to customer cash and crypto. They further alleged that Bankman-Fried directed employees to conceal money flows into FTX and forged financial documents for lenders and investors.

In response, defense lawyer Mark Cohen argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and acted in 'good faith' as a nerdy startup founder, rejecting the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' narrative. The defense maintained that Alameda was a successful hedge fund and FTX an innovative company, not a Ponzi scheme, and claimed legal business practices were followed. Bankman-Fried compared building a startup to flying a plane, citing former Alameda CEO Caroline Ellison for failing to protect the fund from crypto market risks. He argued he was not guilty, stating he built two billion-dollar businesses and did not steal money, offering to give up personal wealth to make customers whole.

Witness testimony began with Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London, who testified that he invested in FTX in 2021, trading Bitcoin and Dogecoin, and failed to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8. Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, testified that he joined Alameda and FTX after Bankman-Fried persuaded him to leave Jane Street; Yedidia claimed legal immunity because he feared his code contributed to a crime. The trial schedule indicated further witnesses were set to appear post-adjournment.

### tech-news/sbf-s-trial-and-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx.md

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the timeline from SBF's co-founding of Alameda and FTX in 2017-2019, through their massive growth and collapse in 2022, to his arrest, trial, and the broader industry fallout.

Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. That same year, FTX bought the naming rights for the Miami Heat's home arena and partnered with celebrities including Tom Brady, Gisele Bündchen, Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal, and Naomi Osaka.

CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest assets were $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. Binance pulled out $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX.

FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. Sam Bankman-Fried resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit, Bankman-Fried stated he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by the events. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation.

During the trial, John J. Ray III testified that FTX had virtually no internal controls or separateness and did not trust a single piece of paper. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. ### tech-news/sbf-s-5b-offer-to-trump-and-ftx-s-rise-and-fall.md

Title: SBF's $5B offer to Trump and FTX's rise and fall
Summary: This note covers Sam Bankman-Fried's reported $5 billion offer to Donald Trump to cancel his presidential run, his background with Michael Lewis, FTX's marketing and trading growth, and the subsequent collapse and legal proceedings.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF), the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of FTX, reportedly offered Donald Trump $5 billion to cancel his presidential re-run; no wire transfer was confirmed. SBF pleaded not guilty to seven charges of fraud and conspiracy in the Manhattan Federal Court trial.

Michael Lewis's book 'Going Infinite' is set to debut on the first day of SBF's trial. Lewis, introduced to SBF in early 2021 by a friend who wanted to back FTX, met SBF more than 100 times over the next two years. Lewis claimed SBF had $22.5 billion eighteen months earlier and was the richest person in the world under 30. 60 Minutes produced a segment featuring SBF shuffling cards and Lewis taking notes on a yellow legal pad. In a 60 Minutes interview, Lewis defended SBF's business practices, claiming FTX would have remained profitable without customer deposit runs.

FTX raised approximately $2 billion, including $1 billion in 2021, from backers including Sequoia, Temasek, and Tiger Global. To lend legitimacy, FTX secured marketing deals with Tom Brady ($55 million) and Steph Curry ($35 million). Anna Wintour contacted SBF via Zoom to sponsor her Met Costume Ball. FTX trading volume climbed to $15 billion per day. SBF also met with Mitch McConnell to fund Republican candidates offsetting Trump's influence.

The company's cryptocurrency valuations fell sharply after being based on speculation rather than banked value. SBF has been denied bail and is widely blamed by crypto investors for losses at Alameda Research and FTX. CEO Ayelet Noff of Sliced Brand criticized SBF, stating he lacked management experience, delayed crypto adoption by 1-2 years, and damaged the community. Financial discrepancies accumulated between FTX exchange and its sister company Alameda Research, leading to FTX's failure.

### tech-news/sbf-s-trial-and-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx.md

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the timeline from SBF's co-founding of Alameda and FTX in 2017-2019, through their massive growth and collapse in 2022, to his arrest, trial, and the broader industry fallout.

Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. That same year, FTX bought the naming rights for the Miami Heat's home arena and partnered with celebrities including Tom Brady, Gisele Bündchen, Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal, and Naomi Osaka.

CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest assets were $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. Binance pulled out $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX.

FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. Sam Bankman-Fried resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit, Bankman-Fried stated he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by the events. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation.

During the trial, John J. Ray III testified that FTX had virtually no internal controls or separateness and did not trust a single piece of paper. U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds, facing up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing in January.
</notes>

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried trial: Opening statements and witness testimony
Summary: A summary of the opening statements and initial witness testimony in the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, covering the prosecution's allegations of fraud and the defense's arguments regarding startup risks and restitution.

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, jury selection concluded, and both sides presented opening statements before witnesses took the stand. Prosecutor Thane Rehn characterized Bankman-Fried as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims, contrasting his public image as a 'crypto boy' genius. Prosecutors argued Bankman-Fried used Alameda Research, a hedge fund he owned, and his girlfriend Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda) as a front to gain secret access to customer cash and crypto. They further alleged that Bankman-Fried directed employees to conceal money flows into FTX and forged financial documents for lenders and investors.

In response, defense lawyer Mark Cohen argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and acted in 'good faith' as a nerdy startup founder, rejecting the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' narrative. The defense maintained that Alameda was a successful hedge fund and FTX an innovative company, not a Ponzi scheme, and claimed legal business practices were followed. Prosecutors argued Bankman-Fried used Alameda Research, a hedge fund he owned, and his girlfriend Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda) as a front to gain secret access to customer cash and crypto. They further alleged that Bankman-Fried directed employees to conceal money flows into FTX and forged financial documents for lenders and investors.

Title: SBF's $5B offer to Trump and FTX's rise and fall
Summary: This note covers Sam Bankman-Fried's reported $5 billion offer to Donald Trump to cancel his presidential run, his background with Michael Lewis, FTX's marketing and trading growth, and the subsequent collapse and legal proceedings.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF), the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of FTX, reportedly offered Donald Trump $5 billion to cancel his presidential re-run; no wire transfer was confirmed. SBF pleaded not guilty to seven charges of fraud and conspiracy in the Manhattan Federal Court trial.

Michael Lewis's book 'Going Infinite' is set to debut on the first day of SBF's trial. Lewis, introduced to SBF in early 2021 by a friend who wanted to back FTX, met SBF more than 100 times over the next two years. Lewis claimed SBF had $22.5 billion eighteen months earlier and was the richest person in the world under 30. 60 Minutes produced a segment featuring SBF shuffling cards and Lewis taking notes on a yellow legal pad. In a 60 Minutes interview, Lewis defended SBF's business practices, claiming FTX would have remained profitable without customer deposit runs.

FTX raised approximately $2 billion, including $1 billion in 2021, from backers including Sequoia, Temasek, and Tiger Global. To lend legitimacy, FTX secured marketing deals with Tom Brady ($55 million) and Steph Curry ($35 million). Anna Wintour contacted SBF via Zoom to sponsor her Met Costume Ball. FTX trading volume climbed to $15 billion per day. SBF also met with Mitch McConnell to fund Republican candidates offsetting Trump's influence.

The company's cryptocurrency valuations fell sharply after being based on speculation rather than banked value. SBF has been denied bail and is widely blamed by crypto investors for losses at Alameda Research and FTX. CEO Ayelet Noff of Sliced Brand criticized SBF, stating he lacked management experience, delayed crypto adoption by 1-2 years, and damaged the community. Financial discrepancies accumulated between FTX exchange and its sister company Alameda Research, leading to FTX's failure.
</notes>

### tech-news/sam-bankman-fried-trial-opening-statements-and-witness.md

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried trial: Opening statements and witness testimony
Summary: A summary of the opening statements and initial witness testimony in the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, covering the prosecution's allegations of fraud and the defense's arguments regarding startup risks and restitution.

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, jury selection concluded, and both sides presented opening statements before witnesses took the stand. Prosecutor Thane Rehn characterized Bankman-Fried as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims, contrasting his public image as a 'crypto boy' genius. Rehn alleged that Bankman-Fried oversaw a thriving FTX exchange, traveled internationally, and socialized with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David while assuring customers their funds were safe. The prosecution claimed Bankman-Fried built this image on lies, allegedly stealing customer funds to finance a jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Prosecutors argued Bankman-Fried used Alameda Research, a hedge fund he owned, and his girlfriend Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda) as a front to gain secret access to customer cash and crypto. They further alleged that Bankman-Fried directed employees to conceal money flows into FTX and forged financial documents for lenders and investors.

In response, defense lawyer Mark Cohen argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and acted in 'good faith' as a nerdy startup founder, rejecting the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' narrative. The defense maintained that Alameda was a successful hedge fund and FTX an innovative company, not a Ponzi scheme, and claimed legal business practices were followed. Bankman-Fried compared building a startup to flying a plane, citing former Alameda CEO Caroline Ellison for failing to protect the fund from crypto market risks. He argued he was not guilty, stating he built two billion-dollar businesses and did not steal money, offering to give up personal wealth to make customers whole.

Witness testimony began with Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London, who testified that he invested in FTX in 2021, trading Bitcoin and Dogecoin, and failed to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8. Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, testified that he joined Alameda and FTX after Bankman-Fried persuaded him to leave Jane Street; Yedidia claimed legal immunity because he feared his code contributed to a crime. The trial schedule indicated further witnesses were set to appear post-adjournment.

### tech-news/sbf-s-trial-and-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx.md

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the timeline from SBF's co-founding of Alameda and FTX in 2017-2019, through their massive growth and collapse in 2022, to his arrest, trial, and the broader industry fallout.

Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. That same year, FTX bought the naming rights for the Miami Heat's home arena and partnered with celebrities including Tom Brady, Gisele Bündchen, Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal, and Naomi Osaka.

CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest assets were $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. Binance pulled out $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX.

FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. Sam Bankman-Fried resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit, Bankman-Fried stated he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by the events. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation.

During the trial, John J. Ray III testified that FTX had virtually no internal controls or separateness and did not trust a single piece of paper. U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds, facing up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing in January.

Title: Tech news roundup: AI startups, Google Pixel 8, and SBF trial updates
Summary: A collection of recent tech developments including Sam Altman's backing of Induced AI, Google's Pixel 8 launch, LinkedIn's AI tools, and updates on the SBF trial and X post volume disputes.

Sam Altman has backed Induced AI, a startup founded this year by two teenagers that automates business workflows by converting plain English instructions to pseudo-code in real time. A review of the Pixel 8 Pro highlights improved cameras, a brighter screen, and enhanced AI features, though it notes an underutilized temperature sensor. LinkedIn launched new AI tools for job hunting, marketing, and sales, including an updated Recruiter platform, an AI Learning coach, and a marketing campaign tool. Chain Reaction and TechCrunch+ have covered the trial, while TechCrunch+ also highlighted Breathe Battery Technologies, a startup developing software to improve lithium-ion battery charging speeds and longevity. On social media, Elon Musk stated X generated 100–200 million posts daily in September, conflicting with CEO Linda Yaccarino's claim of 500 million posts per day. In the startup world, Dave Clark criticized Flexport's founder and board after being ousted as CEO. IronNet, founded in 2014 by former NSA director Keith Alexander, collapsed after failing to gain traction despite raising over $400 million. Esther Rodriguez-Villegas, founder of Acurable, discusses her company's wearable devices for diagnosing and managing respiratory conditions like sleep apnea and epilepsy. Gmail is also set to announce stricter rules for bulk senders starting next year.

### tech-news/sbf-s-5b-offer-to-trump-and-ftx-s-rise-and-fall.md

Title: SBF's $5B offer to Trump and FTX's rise and fall
Summary: This note covers Sam Bankman-Fried's reported $5 billion offer to Donald Trump to cancel his presidential run, his background with Michael Lewis, FTX's marketing and trading growth, and the subsequent collapse and legal proceedings.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF), the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of FTX, reportedly offered Donald Trump $5 billion to cancel his presidential re-run; no wire transfer was confirmed. SBF pleaded not guilty to seven charges of fraud and conspiracy in the Manhattan Federal Court trial.

Michael Lewis's book 'Going Infinite' is set to debut on the first day of SBF's trial. Lewis, introduced to SBF in early 2021 by a friend who wanted to back FTX, met SBF more than 100 times over the next two years. Lewis claimed SBF had $22.5 billion eighteen months earlier and was the richest person in the world under 30. 60 Minutes produced a segment featuring SBF shuffling cards and Lewis taking notes on a yellow legal pad. In a 60 Minutes interview, Lewis defended SBF's business practices, claiming FTX would have remained profitable without customer deposit runs.

FTX raised approximately $2 billion, including $1 billion in 2021, from backers including Sequoia, Temasek, and Tiger Global. To lend legitimacy, FTX secured marketing deals with Tom Brady ($55 million) and Steph Curry ($35 million). Anna Wintour contacted SBF via Zoom to sponsor her Met Costume Ball. FTX trading volume climbed to $15 billion per day. SBF also met with Mitch McConnell to fund Republican candidates offsetting Trump's influence.

The company's cryptocurrency valuations fell sharply after being based on speculation rather than banked value. SBF has been denied bail and is widely blamed by crypto investors for losses at Alameda Research and FTX. CEO Ayelet Noff of Sliced Brand criticized SBF, stating he lacked management experience, delayed crypto adoption by 1-2 years, and damaged the community. Financial discrepancies accumulated between FTX exchange and its sister company Alameda Research, leading to FTX's failure.
</notes>

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried trial: Opening statements and witness testimony
Summary: A summary of the opening statements and initial witness testimony in the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, covering the prosecution's allegations of fraud and the defense's arguments regarding startup risks and restitution.

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, jury selection concluded, and both sides presented opening statements before witnesses took the stand. Prosecutor Thane Rehn characterized Bankman-Fried as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims, contrasting his public image as a 'crypto boy' genius. Rehn alleged that Bankman-Fried oversaw a thriving FTX exchange, traveled internationally, and socialized with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David while assuring customers their funds were safe. The prosecution claimed Bankman-Fried built this image on lies, allegedly stealing customer funds to finance a jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Prosecutors argued Bankman-Fried used Alameda Research, a hedge fund he owned, and his girlfriend Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda) as a front to gain secret access to customer cash and crypto. They further alleged that Bankman-Fried directed employees to conceal money flows into FTX and forged financial documents for lenders and investors.

In response, defense lawyer Mark Cohen argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and acted in 'good faith' as a nerdy startup founder, rejecting the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' narrative. The defense maintained that Alameda was a successful hedge fund and FTX an innovative company, not a Ponzi scheme, and claimed legal business practices were followed. Bankman-Fried compared building a startup to flying a plane, citing former Alameda CEO Caroline Ellison for failing to protect the fund from crypto market risks. He argued he was not guilty, stating he built two billion-dollar businesses and did not steal money, offering to give up personal wealth to make customers whole.

Witness testimony began with Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London, who testified that he invested in FTX in 2021, trading Bitcoin and Dogecoin, and failed to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8. Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, testified that he joined Alameda and FTX after Bankman-Fried persuaded him to leave Jane Street; Yedidia claimed legal immunity because he feared his code contributed to a crime. The trial schedule indicated further witnesses were set to appear post-adjournment.

### tech-news/sbf-s-5b-offer-to-trump-and-ftx-s-rise-and-fall.md

Title: SBF's $5B offer to Trump and FTX's rise and fall
Summary: This note covers Sam Bankman-Fried's reported $5 billion offer to Donald Trump to cancel his presidential run, his background with Michael Lewis, FTX's marketing and trading growth, and the subsequent collapse and legal proceedings.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF), the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of FTX, reportedly offered Donald Trump $5 billion to cancel his presidential re-run; no wire transfer was confirmed. SBF pleaded not guilty to seven charges of fraud and conspiracy in the Manhattan Federal Court trial.

Michael Lewis's book 'Going Infinite' is set to debut on the first day of SBF's trial. Lewis, introduced to SBF in early 2021 by a friend who wanted to back FTX, met SBF more than 100 times over the next two years. Lewis claimed SBF had $22.5 billion eighteen months earlier and was the richest person in the world under 30. 60 Minutes produced a segment featuring SBF shuffling cards and Lewis taking notes on a yellow legal pad. In a 60 Minutes interview, Lewis defended SBF's business practices, claiming FTX would have remained profitable without customer deposit runs.

FTX raised approximately $2 billion, including $1 billion in 2021, from backers including Sequoia, Temasek, and Tiger Global. To lend legitimacy, FTX secured marketing deals with Tom Brady ($55 million) and Steph Curry ($35 million). Anna Wintour contacted SBF via Zoom to sponsor her Met Costume Ball. FTX trading volume climbed to $15 billion per day. SBF also met with Mitch McConnell to fund Republican candidates offsetting Trump's influence.

The company's cryptocurrency valuations fell sharply after being based on speculation rather than banked value. SBF has been denied bail and is widely blamed by crypto investors for losses at Alameda Research and FTX. CEO Ayelet Noff of Sliced Brand criticized SBF, stating he lacked management experience, delayed crypto adoption by 1-2 years, and damaged the community. Financial discrepancies accumulated between FTX exchange and its sister company Alameda Research, leading to FTX's failure.

Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds, facing up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing in January.

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the timeline from SBF's co-founding of Alameda and FTX in 2017-2019, through their massive growth and collapse in 2022, to his arrest, trial, and the broader industry fallout.

Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. That same year, FTX bought the naming rights for the Miami Heat's home arena and partnered with celebrities including Tom Brady, Gisele Bündchen, Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal, and Naomi Osaka.

CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest assets were $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. Binance pulled out $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX.

FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. Sam Bankman-Fried resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit, Bankman-Fried stated he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by the events. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation.

During the trial, John J. Ray III testified that FTX had virtually no internal controls or separateness and did not trust a single piece of paper. U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds, facing up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing in January.

Title: SBF's $5B offer to Trump and FTX's rise and fall
Summary: This note covers Sam Bankman-Fried's reported $5 billion offer to Donald Trump to cancel his presidential run, his background with Michael Lewis, FTX's marketing and trading growth, and the subsequent collapse and legal proceedings.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF), the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of FTX, reportedly offered Donald Trump $5 billion to cancel his presidential re-run; no wire transfer was confirmed. SBF pleaded not guilty to seven charges of fraud and conspiracy in the Manhattan Federal Court trial.

Michael Lewis's book 'Going Infinite' is set to debut on the first day of SBF's trial. Lewis, introduced to SBF in early 2021 by a friend who wanted to back FTX, met SBF more than 100 times over the next two years. Lewis claimed SBF had $22.5 billion eighteen months earlier and was the richest person in the world under 30. 60 Minutes produced a segment featuring SBF shuffling cards and Lewis taking notes on a yellow legal pad. In a 60 Minutes interview, Lewis defended SBF's business practices, claiming FTX would have remained profitable without customer deposit runs.

FTX raised approximately $2 billion, including $1 billion in 2021, from backers including Sequoia, Temasek, and Tiger Global. To lend legitimacy, FTX secured marketing deals with Tom Brady ($55 million) and Steph Curry ($35 million). Anna Wintour contacted SBF via Zoom to sponsor her Met Costume Ball. FTX trading volume climbed to $15 billion per day. SBF also met with Mitch McConnell to fund Republican candidates offsetting Trump's influence.

The company's cryptocurrency valuations fell sharply after being based on speculation rather than banked value. SBF has been denied bail and is widely blamed by crypto investors for losses at Alameda Research and FTX. CEO Ayelet Noff of Sliced Brand criticized SBF, stating he lacked management experience, delayed crypto adoption by 1-2 years, and damaged the community. Financial discrepancies accumulated between FTX exchange and its sister company Alameda Research, leading to FTX's failure.

Title: Helena World Chronicle files antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet
Summary: Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action lawsuit in U.S. District Court in D.C. accusing Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior under the Sherman Act, alleging they siphon off content, readers, and ad revenue through AI and older technologies.

Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas publisher owning two weekly newspapers, filed a class action lawsuit in U.S. District Court in D.C. against Google and Alphabet, alleging anticompetitive behavior under the Sherman Act. The suit claims Google siphons off publisher content, readers, and ad revenue through AI technologies and older methods like Featured Snippets and Search Generative Experience (SGE). The publisher argues that Google's Knowledge Graph, which launched in May 2012 and contained 500 billion facts by 2020, misappropriated data from publishers, causing them to lose billions of dollars. The case cites a 2023 News Media Alliance report and a Washington Post article stating Google's Bard AI was trained on news publications, which were the third-largest category of training data. The suit alleges changing AdSense rates and the improper spoliation of evidence via Google's destruction of chat messages, referencing the recent Epic Games antitrust win. It seeks damages and an injunction requiring Google to obtain publisher consent to use website data for training AI products, including rivals' AI, and allowing opt-out publishers to appear in search results. The U.S. lawsuit coincides with the Justice Department's suit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies. Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act for class-wide monetary and injunctive relief. Hausfeld law firm states Google's scheme causes profound harm to competition, consumers, labor, and a democratic free press. Google recently reached an agreement with the Canadian government to pay $73.5 million annually to news organizations, though negotiations with Meta remain unresolved.

### tech-news/google-antitrust-case-key-facts-and-testimony.md

Title: Google Antitrust Case: Key Facts and Testimony
Summary: Overview of Google's antitrust trial, including CEO testimony, financial data on default search engine deals, chat log destruction, and legal arguments regarding monopoly practices.

The U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google stems from a 2020 claim over its dominance in the online search market, separate from a January filing by the Department of Justice and eight states to halt its anticompetitive scheme. The government argues Google uses platforms and deals to block competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing necessary data. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified, defending tactics including deals to make Google the default search engine, stating that being the default is a desirable business practice, not illegal. 

Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine across platforms, including attempts to preinstall Chrome on iPhones. Approximately $18 billion of this total went directly to Apple, with the deal in place since 2003. Pichai claimed the decision to pay for default status was made with the consumer in mind to gather data and improve the search engine. A 2007 internal email revealed that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they performed 15% more searches, dropping 27% when they switched away.

Regarding preinstallation, Pichai admitted in 2018 to attempting to convince Tim Cook to preinstall Google services on every iOS device to create an inseparable connection between Google and Apple services, though Tim Cook refused. Google also faced accusations in February of systematically destroying internal chat messages despite a litigation hold, though Pichai later took action to change the chat history default to comply. 

Legal arguments highlighted hypocrisy, noting that while Google denounced Microsoft's 2005 default search engine monopoly, Google's own actions worsened the problem. The DOJ argued that changes to defaults worsen issues, as most users do not change defaults, and noted that competitors like DuckDuckGo, Brave, and Bing use similar arguments against Google's deals with Apple. The case is expected to continue for several weeks and is considered the biggest tech antitrust fight since the U.S. trial against Microsoft in the 1990s. If ruled against Google, the company may be required to change behavior and share APIs with third-party developers.
</notes>

Sam Altman has backed Induced AI, a startup founded this year by two teenagers that automates business workflows by converting plain English instructions to pseudo-code in real time. Google unveiled the Pixel 8, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds, Google Assistant, Bard, and Pixel Watch 2 at its annual hardware event. A review of the Pixel 8 Pro highlights improved cameras, a brighter screen, and enhanced AI features, though it notes an underutilized temperature sensor. LinkedIn launched new AI tools for job hunting, marketing, and sales, including an updated Recruiter platform, an AI Learning coach, and a marketing campaign tool. In the legal sphere, Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" details Sam Bankman-Fried's attempt to buy off Trump, debuting on the first day of his trial. The SBF trial in the Southern District of New York continues, with the prosecution accusing Bankman-Fried of fraud while the defense claims good faith. Chain Reaction and TechCrunch+ have covered the trial, while TechCrunch+ also highlighted Breathe Battery Technologies, a startup developing software to improve lithium-ion battery charging speeds and longevity. On social media, Elon Musk stated X generated 100–200 million posts daily in September, conflicting with CEO Linda Yaccarino's claim of 500 million posts per day. In the startup world, Dave Clark criticized Flexport's founder and board after being ousted as CEO. IronNet, founded in 2014 by former NSA director Keith Alexander, collapsed after failing to gain traction despite raising over $400 million. Esther Rodriguez-Villegas, founder of Acurable, discusses her company's wearable devices for diagnosing and managing respiratory conditions like sleep apnea and epilepsy. Gmail is also set to announce stricter rules for bulk senders starting next year.

### tech-news/sam-bankman-fried-trial-opening-statements-and-witness.md

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried trial: Opening statements and witness testimony
Summary: A summary of the opening statements and initial witness testimony in the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, covering the prosecution's allegations of fraud and the defense's arguments regarding startup risks and restitution.

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, jury selection concluded, and both sides presented opening statements before witnesses took the stand. Prosecutor Thane Rehn characterized Bankman-Fried as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims, contrasting his public image as a 'crypto boy' genius. Rehn alleged that Bankman-Fried oversaw a thriving FTX exchange, traveled internationally, and socialized with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David while assuring customers their funds were safe. The prosecution claimed Bankman-Fried built this image on lies, allegedly stealing customer funds to finance a jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Prosecutors argued Bankman-Fried used Alameda Research, a hedge fund he owned, and his girlfriend Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda) as a front to gain secret access to customer cash and crypto. They further alleged that Bankman-Fried directed employees to conceal money flows into FTX and forged financial documents for lenders and investors.

In response, defense lawyer Mark Cohen argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and acted in 'good faith' as a nerdy startup founder, rejecting the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' narrative. The defense maintained that Alameda was a successful hedge fund and FTX an innovative company, not a Ponzi scheme, and claimed legal business practices were followed. Bankman-Fried compared building a startup to flying a plane, citing former Alameda CEO Caroline Ellison for failing to protect the fund from crypto market risks. He argued he was not guilty, stating he built two billion-dollar businesses and did not steal money, offering to give up personal wealth to make customers whole.

Witness testimony began with Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London, who testified that he invested in FTX in 2021, trading Bitcoin and Dogecoin, and failed to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8. Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, testified that he joined Alameda and FTX after Bankman-Fried persuaded him to leave Jane Street; Yedidia claimed legal immunity because he feared his code contributed to a crime. The trial schedule indicated further witnesses were set to appear post-adjournment.

### tech-news/sbf-s-trial-and-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx.md

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the timeline from SBF's co-founding of Alameda and FTX in 2017-2019, through their massive growth and collapse in 2022, to his arrest, trial, and the broader industry fallout.

Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. That same year, FTX bought the naming rights for the Miami Heat's home arena and partnered with celebrities including Tom Brady, Gisele Bündchen, Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal, and Naomi Osaka.

CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest assets were $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. Binance pulled out $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX.

FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. Sam Bankman-Fried resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit, Bankman-Fried stated he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by the events. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation.

During the trial, John J. Ray III testified that FTX had virtually no internal controls or separateness and did not trust a single piece of paper. U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds, facing up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing in January.

### tech-news/sbf-s-5b-offer-to-trump-and-ftx-s-rise-and-fall.md

Title: SBF's $5B offer to Trump and FTX's rise and fall
Summary: This note covers Sam Bankman-Fried's reported $5 billion offer to Donald Trump to cancel his presidential run, his background with Michael Lewis, FTX's marketing and trading growth, and the subsequent collapse and legal proceedings.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF), the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of FTX, reportedly offered Donald Trump $5 billion to cancel his presidential re-run; no wire transfer was confirmed. SBF pleaded not guilty to seven charges of fraud and conspiracy in the Manhattan Federal Court trial.

Michael Lewis's book 'Going Infinite' is set to debut on the first day of SBF's trial. Lewis, introduced to SBF in early 2021 by a friend who wanted to back FTX, met SBF more than 100 times over the next two years. Lewis claimed SBF had $22.5 billion eighteen months earlier and was the richest person in the world under 30. 60 Minutes produced a segment featuring SBF shuffling cards and Lewis taking notes on a yellow legal pad. In a 60 Minutes interview, Lewis defended SBF's business practices, claiming FTX would have remained profitable without customer deposit runs.

FTX raised approximately $2 billion, including $1 billion in 2021, from backers including Sequoia, Temasek, and Tiger Global. To lend legitimacy, FTX secured marketing deals with Tom Brady ($55 million) and Steph Curry ($35 million). Anna Wintour contacted SBF via Zoom to sponsor her Met Costume Ball. FTX trading volume climbed to $15 billion per day. SBF also met with Mitch McConnell to fund Republican candidates offsetting Trump's influence.

The company's cryptocurrency valuations fell sharply after being based on speculation rather than banked value. SBF has been denied bail and is widely blamed by crypto investors for losses at Alameda Research and FTX. CEO Ayelet Noff of Sliced Brand criticized SBF, stating he lacked management experience, delayed crypto adoption by 1-2 years, and damaged the community. Financial discrepancies accumulated between FTX exchange and its sister company Alameda Research, leading to FTX's failure.
</notes>

### tech-news/helena-world-chronicle-files-antitrust-suit-against-google.md

Title: Helena World Chronicle files antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet
Summary: Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action lawsuit in U.S. District Court in D.C. accusing Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior under the Sherman Act, alleging they siphon off content, readers, and ad revenue through AI and older technologies.

Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas publisher owning two weekly newspapers, filed a class action lawsuit in U.S. District Court in D.C. against Google and Alphabet, alleging anticompetitive behavior under the Sherman Act. The suit claims Google siphons off publisher content, readers, and ad revenue through AI technologies and older methods like Featured Snippets and Search Generative Experience (SGE). The publisher argues that Google's Knowledge Graph, which launched in May 2012 and contained 500 billion facts by 2020, misappropriated data from publishers, causing them to lose billions of dollars. The case cites a 2023 News Media Alliance report and a Washington Post article stating Google's Bard AI was trained on news publications, which were the third-largest category of training data. The suit alleges changing AdSense rates and the improper spoliation of evidence via Google's destruction of chat messages, referencing the recent Epic Games antitrust win. It seeks damages and an injunction requiring Google to obtain publisher consent to use website data for training AI products, including rivals' AI, and allowing opt-out publishers to appear in search results. The U.S. lawsuit coincides with the Justice Department's suit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies. Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act for class-wide monetary and injunctive relief. Hausfeld law firm states Google's scheme causes profound harm to competition, consumers, labor, and a democratic free press. Google recently reached an agreement with the Canadian government to pay $73.5 million annually to news organizations, though negotiations with Meta remain unresolved.
</notes>

### tech-news/sbf-s-trial-and-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx.md

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the timeline from SBF's co-founding of Alameda and FTX in 2017-2019, through their massive growth and collapse in 2022, to his arrest, trial, and the broader industry fallout.

Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. That same year, FTX bought the naming rights for the Miami Heat's home arena and partnered with celebrities including Tom Brady, Gisele Bündchen, Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal, and Naomi Osaka.

CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest assets were $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. Binance pulled out $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX.

FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. Sam Bankman-Fried resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit, Bankman-Fried stated he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by the events. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation.

During the trial, John J. Ray III testified that FTX had virtually no internal controls or separateness and did not trust a single piece of paper. U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds, facing up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing in January.
</notes>

Title: SBF's $5B offer to Trump and FTX's rise and fall
Summary: This note covers Sam Bankman-Fried's reported $5 billion offer to Donald Trump to cancel his presidential run, his background with Michael Lewis, FTX's marketing and trading growth, and the subsequent collapse and legal proceedings.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF), the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of FTX, reportedly offered Donald Trump $5 billion to cancel his presidential re-run; no wire transfer was confirmed. SBF pleaded not guilty to seven charges of fraud and conspiracy in the Manhattan Federal Court trial.

Michael Lewis's book 'Going Infinite' is set to debut on the first day of SBF's trial. Lewis, introduced to SBF in early 2021 by a friend who wanted to back FTX, met SBF more than 100 times over the next two years. Lewis claimed SBF had $22.5 billion eighteen months earlier and was the richest person in the world under 30. 60 Minutes produced a segment featuring SBF shuffling cards and Lewis taking notes on a yellow legal pad. In a 60 Minutes interview, Lewis defended SBF's business practices, claiming FTX would have remained profitable without customer deposit runs.

FTX raised approximately $2 billion, including $1 billion in 2021, from backers including Sequoia, Temasek, and Tiger Global. To lend legitimacy, FTX secured marketing deals with Tom Brady ($55 million) and Steph Curry ($35 million). Anna Wintour contacted SBF via Zoom to sponsor her Met Costume Ball. FTX trading volume climbed to $15 billion per day. SBF also met with Mitch McConnell to fund Republican candidates offsetting Trump's influence.

The company's cryptocurrency valuations fell sharply after being based on speculation rather than banked value. SBF has been denied bail and is widely blamed by crypto investors for losses at Alameda Research and FTX. CEO Ayelet Noff of Sliced Brand criticized SBF, stating he lacked management experience, delayed crypto adoption by 1-2 years, and damaged the community. Financial discrepancies accumulated between FTX exchange and its sister company Alameda Research, leading to FTX's failure.

### tech-news/sam-bankman-fried-trial-opening-statements-and-witness.md

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried trial: Opening statements and witness testimony
Summary: A summary of the opening statements and initial witness testimony in the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, covering the prosecution's allegations of fraud and the defense's arguments regarding startup risks and restitution.

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, jury selection concluded, and both sides presented opening statements before witnesses took the stand. Prosecutor Thane Rehn characterized Bankman-Fried as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims, contrasting his public image as a 'crypto boy' genius. Rehn alleged that Bankman-Fried oversaw a thriving FTX exchange, traveled internationally, and socialized with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David while assuring customers their funds were safe. The prosecution claimed Bankman-Fried built this image on lies, allegedly stealing customer funds to finance a jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Prosecutors argued Bankman-Fried used Alameda Research, a hedge fund he owned, and his girlfriend Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda) as a front to gain secret access to customer cash and crypto. They further alleged that Bankman-Fried directed employees to conceal money flows into FTX and forged financial documents for lenders and investors.

In response, defense lawyer Mark Cohen argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and acted in 'good faith' as a nerdy startup founder, rejecting the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' narrative. The defense maintained that Alameda was a successful hedge fund and FTX an innovative company, not a Ponzi scheme, and claimed legal business practices were followed. Bankman-Fried compared building a startup to flying a plane, citing former Alameda CEO Caroline Ellison for failing to protect the fund from crypto market risks. He argued he was not guilty, stating he built two billion-dollar businesses and did not steal money, offering to give up personal wealth to make customers whole.

Witness testimony began with Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London, who testified that he invested in FTX in 2021, trading Bitcoin and Dogecoin, and failed to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8. Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, testified that he joined Alameda and FTX after Bankman-Fried persuaded him to leave Jane Street; Yedidia claimed legal immunity because he feared his code contributed to a crime. The trial schedule indicated further witnesses were set to appear post-adjournment.

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest assets were $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. Binance pulled out $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX.

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, jury selection concluded, and both sides presented opening statements before witnesses took the stand. Rehn alleged that Bankman-Fried oversaw a thriving FTX exchange, traveled internationally, and socialized with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David while assuring customers their funds were safe. The prosecution claimed Bankman-Fried built this image on lies, allegedly stealing customer funds to finance a jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Prosecutors argued Bankman-Fried used Alameda Research, a hedge fund he owned, and his girlfriend Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda) as a front to gain secret access to customer cash and crypto. Title: Google Antitrust Case: Key Facts and Testimony
Summary: Overview of Google's antitrust trial, including CEO testimony, financial data on default search engine deals, chat log destruction, and legal arguments regarding monopoly practices.

The U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google stems from a 2020 claim over its dominance in the online search market, separate from a January filing by the Department of Justice and eight states to halt its anticompetitive scheme. The government argues Google uses platforms and deals to block competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing necessary data. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified, defending tactics including deals to make Google the default search engine, stating that being the default is a desirable business practice, not illegal. 

Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine across platforms, including attempts to preinstall Chrome on iPhones. Approximately $18 billion of this total went directly to Apple, with the deal in place since 2003. Pichai claimed the decision to pay for default status was made with the consumer in mind to gather data and improve the search engine. A 2007 internal email revealed that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they performed 15% more searches, dropping 27% when they switched away.

Regarding preinstallation, Pichai admitted in 2018 to attempting to convince Tim Cook to preinstall Google services on every iOS device to create an inseparable connection between Google and Apple services, though Tim Cook refused. Google also faced accusations in February of systematically destroying internal chat messages despite a litigation hold, though Pichai later took action to change the chat history default to comply. 

Legal arguments highlighted hypocrisy, noting that while Google denounced Microsoft's 2005 default search engine monopoly, Google's own actions worsened the problem. The DOJ argued that changes to defaults worsen issues, as most users do not change defaults, and noted that competitors like DuckDuckGo, Brave, and Bing use similar arguments against Google's deals with Apple. The case is expected to continue for several weeks and is considered the biggest tech antitrust fight since the U.S. trial against Microsoft in the 1990s. If ruled against Google, the company may be required to change behavior and share APIs with third-party developers.

The U.S. lawsuit coincides with the Justice Department's suit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies. Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act for class-wide monetary and injunctive relief.
